overview: A ridge gives way to a series of Pacific fronts from Monday on, bringing mountain snow and rain to the Cascades and Sierra, while British Columbia's Coast Mountains get more rain and mixed precipitation than deep snow.

regions.title: Cascades
regions.text: A weak system brings light snow showers to the Cascades this weekend, then a stronger front arrives Monday and stays through Tuesday. Crystal Mountain leads the region with 19 inches over the five days, with its biggest day Tuesday at 10 inches. Snow levels hover near 2,500 feet, so the snow is light but steady.

regions.title: Coast Mountains
regions.text: Environment Canada shows the snow here is brief. Whistler gets 19 inches over the window, peaking at 8 inches Tuesday, but rain takes over Tuesday night and continues into Wednesday. Cypress Mountain sees mostly rain and totals 5 inches. Expect wet, heavy snow at the top and rain lower down.

regions.title: Tahoe
regions.text: A weak system crosses the Sierra Sunday with light snow above 4,000 feet. Sugar Bowl and Palisades get the most, about 6 to 9 inches. A break comes Monday before a stronger system arrives mid-week. The NWS is calling for more, 11 to 21 inches at Sugar Bowl and 9 to 22 inches at Palisades, Sunday through Wednesday night.

sources.name: NOAA buoys 51001 / 51101 (method: Powder Buoy, Mike Ruzek)

buoy.text: Buoys 51001 and 51101 near Hawaii popped Nov 11, the swell signal Powder Buoy watches for a Wasatch storm about two weeks later — here Nov 22–28. In past winters a pop raised the chance of a Wasatch storm in that window by roughly 6 to 12 points. Experimental: promising, not proven.
